# EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning

Chen Affiliation: National University of Singapore    Yue Liu

###### Abstract

Prevailing medical AI operates on an unrealistic “one-shot” model,
diagnosing from a complete patient file. However, real-world diagnosis
is an iterative inquiry where Clinicians sequentially ask questions and
order tests to strategically gather information while managing cost and
time. To address this, we first propose Med-Inquire, a new benchmark
designed to evaluate an agent’s ability to perform multi-turn diagnosis.
Built upon a dataset of real-world clinical cases, Med-Inquire simulates
the diagnostic process by hiding a complete patient file behind
specialized Patient and Examination agents. They force the agent to
proactively ask questions and order tests to gather information piece by
piece. To tackle the challenges posed by Med-Inquire, we then introduce
EvoClinician, a self-evolving agent that learns efficient diagnostic
strategies at test time. Its core is a “Diagnose-Grade-Evolve” loop: an
Actor agent attempts a diagnosis; a Process Grader agent performs credit
assignment by evaluating each action for both clinical yield and
resource efficiency; finally, an Evolver agent uses this feedback to
update the Actor’s strategy by evolving its prompt and memory. Our
experiments show EvoClinician outperforms continual learning baselines
and other self-evolving agents like memory agents. The code is available
at
[https://github.com/yf-he/EvoClinician](https://github.com/yf-he/EvoClinician)

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

The application of artificial intelligence in medicine holds immense
promise for clinical decision-making ([Cabral et al., 2024](#bib.bib4);
[Nori et al., 2023](#bib.bib1); [Gilson et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)).
However, a prevailing paradigm for medical AI operates on an unrealistic
“one-shot” model, where an agent is fed a complete patient file—with all
history, findings, and lab results—to produce a diagnosis ([Nori et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1)). This static, complete-information approach stands in
contrast to real-world clinical practice. A clinician’s work is not a
single calculation but a dynamic and iterative process of inquiry ([Nori
et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). They begin with a chief complaint and
sequentially ask targeted questions, perform physical exams, and order
specific tests to strategically gather information, all while
judiciously managing constraints of cost and time ([Li et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib9); [Liberatore and Nydick, 2008](#bib.bib32)). This
procedural skill of balancing diagnostic accuracy with resource
efficiency is the sign of an expert clinician, yet it is a capability
largely absent in today’s medical AI systems ([Nori et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)).

Existing benchmarks primarily measure final diagnostic accuracy, failing
to reward or even quantify an agent’s efficiency in arriving at that
diagnosis ([Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib36); [Wang et al.,
2024c](#bib.bib37); [Ye et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)). To provide a more
realistic measure of clinical ability, we introduce Med-Inquire, a
benchmark built upon real-world clinical cases. It enforces a sequential
diagnostic workflow by concealing the complete patient file behind
specialized Patient and Examination agents. This “gatekeeper” design
compels agents to learn the skill of proactive inquiry, gathering
information piece by piece as a human clinician would. The agent’s
performance is assessed by two key components. A Judge Agent compares
the submitted diagnosis against the ground truth, assigning a score that
reflects its correctness. Simultaneously, a Cost Estimator agent tracks
the cumulative cost of the clinical encounter.

To this end, we introduce EvoClinician, a self-evolving agent that
learns efficient diagnostic strategies by treating each unique case in
the Med-Inquire benchmark sequentially as a distinct, test-time learning
opportunity. The agent’s learning process is a “Diagnose-Grade-Evolve”
loop, driven by an internal multi-agent architecture.

First, in the Diagnose phase, an Actor agent, guided by its current
prompt and memory, attempts to diagnose a new case. It interacts with
the Med-Inquire environment, asking questions and ordering tests until
it decides to submit a final diagnosis. The full transcript of this
interaction, including every action and its outcome, is logged.

Next, the Grade phase solves the difficult credit assignment problem
inherent in long-horizon tasks. Instead of relying on a single, sparse
reward from the final judgment, a Process Grader agent performs a
detailed post-session review. It analyzes the full transcript, the final
judgment, and the cost report to generate a dense feedback signal. It
assigns a qualitative grade (e.g., ‘HIGH_YIELD’, ‘LOW_YIELD’,
‘INEFFICIENT’, ‘CRITICAL_ERROR’) and a rationale to each individual
action taken by the Actor. This transforms the evaluation from a simple
trajectory-level score into an action-level critique.

Finally, in the Evolve phase, this granular feedback is used to create
lasting improvements. An Evolver agent takes the action-level critiques
from the Process Grader and performs a gradient-free update on the
Actor’s core strategy. This update is twofold, modifying both the
agent’s high-level strategic guidance (its prompt) and its specific
experiential knowledge (its memory).

For Prompt Evolution, the Evolver translates the action-level grades
into permanent changes in the Actor’s prompt. High-yield actions are
abstracted into generalizable instructions for future use, teaching the
agent what to do. For example, a successful early question might become
a new rule: “If a patient has a scalp lump, always ask if it has been
present since birth.” Conversely, inefficient or erroneous actions are
used to teach the agent what not to do. For Memory Evolution, it
captures both positive and negative experiences at the action level. The
Evolver processes significant action from the session. It creates a
discrete memory entry that includes: the clinical context (the state)
before the action, the action itself, the resulting new information (the
outcome), and the grade it received. This creates a rich repository of
both effective and bad moves. In subsequent cases, when the Actor faces
a similar clinical context, it can retrieve relevant memories.

More generally, the same methodology applies to any domain where an
agent must plan, use tools, and make decisions under limits (time,
money, risk, or compute), and where feedback is not immediately and
delayed across many steps. For example, in customer service the agent
must choose among clarification, policy lookup, account actions, and
escalation while balancing resolution quality and handle time. In
financial management, an agent may choose data pulls, checks, and
transaction proposals while controlling risk and fees, with constraints
such as budgets and compliance rules. In each case, one can build an
interactive environment with domain-specific tools and constraints,
define a task-level score and a resource report, and then use
action-level critiques to update reusable rules and memory.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

- •
  We introduce Med-Inquire, an interactive benchmark for multi-turn
  medical diagnosis that hides the full case file behind Patient and
  Examination agents and evaluates both diagnosis grade and resource
  cost.
- •
  We propose EvoClinician, a test-time learning agent with a
  Diagnose-Grade-Evolve loop that uses action-level grading to update
  prompt and memory between cases.
- •
  We compare against static prompting, memory agents, prompt
  optimization methods, and prior self-evolving agents, and we show that
  our approach improves outcome quality while reducing resource use.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Medical Agents

Most medical language model evaluations are still based on static exam
questions, which bundle history and examination results into one input.
This style has been used in many studies of medical question answering
and diagnostic reasoning, including work reporting strong performance on
medical challenge problems and licensing style tests ([Nori et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1); [Singhal et al., 2022](#bib.bib2); [Gilson et al.,
2022](#bib.bib3); [Cabral et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)). Related interactive
medical work studies question-asking as a first-class decision
problem([Gorry and Barnett, 1968](#bib.bib7); [Horvitz et al.,
1988](#bib.bib8)). MedIQ ([Li et al., 2024b](#bib.bib5)) evaluates
question-asking LLMs for interactive clinical reasoning. SDBench ([Nori
et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)), built from NEJM clinicopathological
conference cases, evaluates both diagnostic correctness and cost.

There is also a growing body of work on multi-agent clinical simulation,
where doctor, patient, and tool roles interact in a simulated setting.
These systems are often used for studying dialogue quality,
coordination, and training data generation ([Li et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib9); [Almansoori et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib11)). AgentClinic ([Schmidgall et al., 2024](#bib.bib12))
is another related direction that benchmarks multimodal agents in
simulated clinical environments. Compared with these simulation systems,
Med-Inquire is designed for measuring sequential diagnostic policies
with a reproducible cost model and a diagnosis grading rubric.

![Refer to caption](2601.22964v1/arch.png)

Figure 1: EvoClinician architecture and test-time learning loop. The
Actor interacts with the Med-Inquire environment through AskQuestion and
OrderTest, receiving responses from the Patient and Examination agents,
while the Cost Estimator tracks resource use. After SubmitDiagnosis, the
Judge assigns a graded correctness score. The Process Grader then
reviews the full transcript and assigns action-level labels (for
example, HIGH YIELD, LOW YIELD, INEFFICIENT) for credit assignment.
Finally, the Evolver uses these labels, the final score, and the cost
report to update the Actor’s prompt rules and external memory before the
next episode, forming a repeated Diagnose–Grade–Evolve loop over a
stream of cases at test time.

### 2.2 Self-Evolving Agents

Self-evolving agents update their behavior based on experience, rather
than running with a fixed prompt and no persistent state ([Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib20); [Xi et al., 2025](#bib.bib13); [He et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib51); [Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Hu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib57); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib54)). A common mechanism
is long-term memory that stores past interactions and retrieves relevant
items for new tasks. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a
general template for adding external memory to language model inference
([Lewis et al., 2020](#bib.bib21); [He et al., 2025a](#bib.bib19); [He
et al., 2025d](#bib.bib43); [He et al., 2025e](#bib.bib48); [He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53)). More agent-specific memory systems include Mem0,
which maintains memory with add, merge, and delete operations, and
trajectory-based methods that turn experience into reusable guidance
([Chhikara et al., 2025](#bib.bib22); [Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib23);
[Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib58); [Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib52); [Chen
et al., 2025d](#bib.bib55)). Workflow-level memory stores reusable
action plans rather than raw text, aiming to improve multi-step behavior
([Wang et al., 2024d](#bib.bib24)). These methods often help reuse
information, but they do not always change the agent policy in a stable
way, because the main policy still comes from a fixed prompt.

Another line of work updates prompts or rules. Prompt optimization can
be cast as search over instruction text, including evolutionary prompt
methods such as PromptBreeder([Fernando et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)), and
other automatic prompt optimization frameworks ([Pryzant et al.,
2023](#bib.bib25); [Yang et al., 2023](#bib.bib15)). Some approaches use
language feedback as an update signal for prompts or intermediate
reasoning steps, including TextGrad ([Yuksekgonul et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)). Reflection-based methods store critiques of failures
and use them to guide later attempts, for example Reflexion and
Self-Refine ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)). These methods give denser guidance than a single
final score, but they often do not perform action-level credit
assignment for long trajectories with costs ([He et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib31)).

Reinforcement learning methods for agents address sequential decision
making more directly, but the learning signal is often sparse and hard
to assign to individual actions ([Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Liu
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib45); [Sui et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50); [Sui et al., 2024b](#bib.bib47); [Sui et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib49)). Recent work studies multi-turn reinforcement
learning for LLM agents and strategy learning from interaction,
including RAGEN ([Wang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib27)) and DYSTIL ([Wang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib28)). Separate work on process supervision and step
verification shows that intermediate feedback can improve long-horizon
reasoning, including Let’s Verify Step by Step ([Lightman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib29)) and Math-Shepherd ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib30)).
EvoClinician adopts the same general idea of denser feedback, but
applies it to clinical actions (questions and tests) and adds resource
efficiency to the grading signal.

## 3 Benchmark: Med-Inquire

### 3.1 Task Definition

Med-Inquire is an interactive diagnosis task. Each episode corresponds
to one real-world clinical case with a hidden full patient file. The
agent starts with only an initial problem statement (for example, a
chief complaint and basic demographics when available). The agent then
takes actions to gather more information. At any time, the agent may
stop and submit a final diagnosis.

We model the interaction as a partially observable Markov decision
process (POMDP). The hidden state is the complete case file. The agent
observes only the information returned by the environment in response to
its actions. This structure matches the key limitation of clinical care:
the clinician does not observe the full state and must choose what to
ask or order next.

### 3.2 Environment Design and Information Gatekeeping

Med-Inquire hides the case file behind two environment components that
we implement as constrained agents.

The Patient agent answers questions in the style of a real patient. It
responds to queries about symptoms, medical history, and related context
(for example, onset time, triggers, and prior conditions) using only
information recorded in the hidden case file. If the case file does not
contain the requested detail, it generates a medically reasonable
patient-style answer that is consistent with the ground-truth diagnosis
and with information already revealed in the dialogue, rather than
returning an “unknown/not documented” response.

The Examination agent returns results for physical examination findings
and diagnostic tests. Tests include both low-cost screening tests and
higher-cost confirmatory tests, when those are represented in the case
file. If an agent orders a test that is not present in the case file,
the Examination agent returns “not available”.

### 3.3 Action Space and Interaction Protocol

At each turn $`t`$, the agent chooses one action $`a_{t}`$ from three
types.

First, AskQuestion: a free-form question to the Patient agent. The
environment returns a text answer grounded in the case file.

Second, OrderTest: a request to the Examination agent for a named
examination maneuver or diagnostic test. The environment returns the
recorded test result, if present, and otherwise returns a null response
as described above.

Third, SubmitDiagnosis: the agent submits a final diagnosis. This action
ends the episode.

To make evaluation reproducible, we set a fixed maximum number of turns
$`T_{\max}`$. We log the full transcript: all actions, all environment
responses, and the final submission.

### 3.4 Cost Model

Med-Inquire assigns a non-negative cost to each action to reflect
resource use. Let $`c(a_{t})`$ be the cost of action $`a_{t}`$. The
total encounter cost is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       C=\sum_{t=1}^{T}c(a_{t}),
       ```                        |     | (1) |

where $`T`$ is the number of turns until the episode ends.

Costs include at least (i) a base per-turn interaction cost (time and
clinician effort) and (ii) a test-specific cost for each ordered test.
In our implementation, the cost schedule is provided as a table that
maps test names to costs, along with a default cost for free-form
questioning. The benchmark reports costs in the same unit across all
cases (normalized cost units), because exact billing varies by setting
and country. Users who want a different schedule can swap the cost table
without changing the rest of the benchmark, as long as the mapping is
reported.

### 3.5 Diagnosis Judging

After SubmitDiagnosis, a Judge agent compares the submitted diagnosis
against the ground-truth diagnosis recorded in the hidden case file. The
Judge agent outputs a graded correctness score $`S\in[0,100]`$, where
higher values mean closer agreement with the ground truth. The Judge
agent uses a single graded mode. It then evaluates clinical agreement
between the submission and the ground truth using the rubric in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Diagnosis judging ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning").

### 3.6 Benchmark Metrics

Med-Inquire evaluates an agent along three axes: diagnostic grade,
interaction length, and resource cost. For each episode $`i`$, the
benchmark records (i) the Judge grade $`S_{i}\in[0,100]`$, (ii) the
number of turns $`T_{i}`$, and (iii) the total encounter cost $`C_{i}`$.
The diagnostic grade $`S_{i}`$ measures how closely the submitted
diagnosis matches the ground-truth diagnosis under the rubric in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Diagnosis judging ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning").
The number of turns $`T_{i}`$ counts all actions taken until the agent
submits a diagnosis. The cost $`C_{i}`$ is the sum of per-action costs.

## 4 Method: EvoClinician

### 4.1 Test-Time Learning Setting

We use the term _test-time learning_ (TTL) ([He et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib19); [He et al., 2025c](#bib.bib31)) to indicate any
method that updates its internal state during evaluation, after
deployment of the base model, using only information available from the
test-time interaction. In our setting, the agent faces a sequence of
diagnosis episodes $`\{1,\dots,N\}`$ from Med-Inquire. During episode
$`i`$, the agent can only observe (1) the initial case presentation, (2)
responses from the Patient and Examination agents to its actions, (3)
the final Judge score $`S_{i}\in[0,100]`$, and (4) the total cost
$`C_{i}`$. The agent does not receive the hidden case file or the
ground-truth diagnosis information.

We study TTL where the agent updates _prompts_ and _external memory_
between episodes. We do not update the weights of the base LLMs.

### 4.2 Overview

As shown in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Medical Agents ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning"),
EvoClinician is a multi-agent system that runs a repeated
Diagnose–Grade–Evolve loop. It has three internal roles.

First, an Actor interacts with the Med-Inquire environment to gather
information and then submits a diagnosis.

Second, a Process Grader reads the full transcript, the final Judge
score, and the cost report, and then assigns action-level feedback. This
feedback is meant to address credit assignment: it links later success
or failure to earlier questions and tests.

Third, an Evolver updates the Actor’s strategy for future episodes. The
Evolver edits (i) the Actor prompt, which acts as persistent high-level
guidance, and (ii) an external memory, which stores action advice with
labels.

### 4.3 Actor

The Actor is an LLM agent with a system prompt $`P`$ and a memory $`M`$.
At turn $`t`$, the Actor receives the dialogue history $`h_{t}`$ and
retrieves a small set of relevant memories

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathcal{R}_{t}=\mathrm{Retrieve}(M,h_{t};k),
       ```                                            |     | (2) |

where $`k`$ is a fixed retrieval count.

The Actor then chooses an action
$`a_{t}\in\{\texttt{AskQuestion},\texttt{OrderTest},\texttt{SubmitDiagnosis}\}`$
and produces natural-language content for that action (the question, the
test name, or the diagnosis). The environment returns an observation
$`o_{t+1}`$ and the running cost increases by $`c(a_{t})`$. The episode
ends when the Actor chooses SubmitDiagnosis or reaches $`T_{\max}`$.

We do not assume that the Actor has access to a fixed list of allowed
tests. Instead, the Actor proposes a test name in text, and the
Examination agent either returns a recorded result or “not available”.
This makes the action space open-ended and places weight on planning
rather than list lookup.

### 4.4 Process Grader (action-level feedback)

After the episode ends, the Process Grader receives the transcript

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \tau_{i}=\{(h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1})\}_{t=1}^{T_{i}},
       ```                                                |     | (3) |

the final Judge score $`S_{i}`$, and the total cost $`C_{i}`$. It
outputs a set of per-action labels and short rationales:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       G_{i}=\{(g_{t},r_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T_{i}}.
       ```                                     |     | (4) |

Each label $`g_{t}`$ is chosen from a small set such as HIGH_YIELD,
LOW_YIELD, INEFFICIENT, and CRITICAL_ERROR. The grader uses two
criteria.

First, _clinical yield_: whether the action reduced diagnostic
uncertainty given the state of the dialogue at that time. For example, a
targeted question that separates two likely diagnoses can be high yield.

Second, _resource efficiency_: whether the same information could likely
have been obtained with lower cost or fewer steps. For example, ordering
a costly confirmatory test before basic screening can be graded as
inefficient, even if it returns helpful information.

The Process Grader also produces a brief session summary that states why
the final diagnosis achieved score $`S_{i}`$ and which earlier steps
helped or harmed performance. A theory view of the Process Grader is
given in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Theory: Process Grader for Action-Level Feedback ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning").

### 4.5 Evolver (prompt and memory updates)

The Evolver takes $`(\tau_{i},S_{i},C_{i},G_{i})`$ and updates the Actor
prompt $`P`$ and memory $`M`$ with a gradient-free procedure.

Prompt evolution. We represent the Actor prompt as a base instruction
plus a list of short rules. After episode $`i`$, the Evolver proposes
edits to this rule list. Each edit is derived from the graded
transcript.

When the grader marks an action as HIGH_YIELD, the Evolver may add a
rule that generalizes the pattern, conditioned on the observed context.
The rule form is constrained to be short and operational, for example,
“If symptom X and time course Y, ask about Z before ordering imaging.”

When the grader marks an action as INEFFICIENT or CRITICAL_ERROR, the
Evolver may add a guard rule that blocks similar actions in similar
contexts, for example, “Before ordering test T, state what decision it
changes and whether a cheaper test could answer the same question.”

To reduce drift, we use two constraints. First, the prompt has a maximum
rule budget $`B_{P}`$; if the budget is exceeded, the Evolver removes or
merges the lowest-utility rules based on how often the grader cited them
in recent episodes. Second, the Evolver does not add rules that mention
case-specific identifiers; it rewrites them into general clinical
features (for example, “acute chest pain” rather than a named patient).

Memory evolution. Memory stores case-conditioned action advice. From the
transcript, the Evolver selects a subset of turns $`\mathcal{T}_{i}`$
that have strong feedback (for example, HIGH*YIELD or CRITICAL_ERROR).
For each selected turn $`t\in\mathcal{T}*{i}`$, it writes a memory entry

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       m=\big(\phi(h_{t}),a_{t},o_{t+1},g_{t},r_{t}\big),
       ```                                                 |     | (5) |

where $`\phi(h_{t})`$ is a compressed representation of the clinical
context extracted from the dialogue history (key symptoms, time course,
and already-known test results). At the start of each new turn,
retrieval returns entries with similar $`\phi(h_{t})`$, and the Actor
uses their actions and grades as suggestions or warnings. Memory has a
maximum size $`B_{M}`$. When full, we delete entries with low expected
reuse, measured by a combination of age and retrieval frequency.

![Refer to caption](2601.22964v1/learning_curves_running.png)

Figure 2: Running-mean learning curves on Med-Inquire over $`N=915`$
cases (fixed evaluation order). Left: running mean Judge grade
$`\bar{S}_{1:t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}S_{i}`$, where
$`S_{i}\in[0,100]`$ is the per-case diagnosis grade. Right: running mean
cost $`\bar{C}_{1:t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}C_{i}`$, where $`C_{i}`$
is the per-case cumulative cost in normalized units from the fixed cost
table. Faint points show per-case values, and lines show the running
mean. Shaded bands show an approximate $`95\%`$ interval based on the
running standard error, $`\bar{x}_{1:t}\pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}_{1:t}`$,
computed from the first $`t`$ cases.

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Dataset

The patient cases come from DiagnosisArena ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)), which is a collection of 915 real-world medical
cases taken from reports published in 10 major medical journals like The
New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) and The Lancet. Each case in the
dataset is organized into four main parts: Case Information (the
patient’s background, Physical Examination (the results of check-up),
Diagnostic Tests (results from labs), and the Final Diagnosis.

### 5.2 Setup

For methods that update at test time, we evaluate cases in a fixed order
and allow updates only between episodes. We run experiments with four
base LLM backbones: gemini-3-pro ([Team et al., 2023](#bib.bib39)),
gpt-5.1 ([Singh et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)), gpt-4o-mini ([Hurst et al.,
2024](#bib.bib41)), and MedGemma-27b ([Sellergren et al.,
2025](#bib.bib42)). We run each method with the same $`T_{\max}`$ and
the same stopping condition: the agent may submit a diagnosis at any
time. If the agent reaches $`T_{\max}`$ without submitting, we force
SubmitDiagnosis using the agent’s current best guess.

### 5.3 Baselines

We compare three baseline categories: static prompt, memory agent, and
prompt optimization agent. All baselines use the same base LLM, decoding
settings, and setup (including the same $`T_{\max}`$).

The static prompt baseline is (1) Static Prompt, which uses one fixed
system prompt for all episodes and stores no cross-episode state.

The memory agent baselines keep the prompt fixed but add long-term
memory across episodes: (2) Memory Agent, which fills the context window
with full past transcripts and drops the oldest first when reaching the
token limit; (3) RAG ([Lewis et al., 2020](#bib.bib21)), which retrieves
top-$`k`$ chunked past text from a vector index; (4) Mem0 ([Chhikara et
al., 2025](#bib.bib22)), which extracts and consolidates memory items
and retrieves them when needed; and (5) Evo-Memory ([Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)), which update memory between episodes (experience
retrieval and memory refine variants) without updating the main prompt.

The prompt optimization agent baselines update the system prompt for
future episodes: (6) EvoPrompt ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), which
searches for an improved prompt on a held-out development subset and
then freezes it for evaluation; and (7) GEPA ([Agrawal et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35)), which is a prompt optimizer that incorporates
natural language reflection to learn high-level rules from trial and
error.

The evolutionary agent (8) EvoTest ([He et al., 2025c](#bib.bib31)),
which updates the agent configuration (including the prompt, memory)
after each episode using transcript-level feedback.

### 5.4 Evaluation

We evaluate all methods under the test-time learning (TTL) setting in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Test-Time Learning Setting ‣ 4 Method: EvoClinician ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning").
Only the TTL methods are allowed to adapt across episodes (by updating
prompt state and or external memory between episodes). Non-TTL baselines
keep their prompt and memory fixed for all cases.

For each episode $`i`$, Med-Inquire returns the Judge diagnostic grade
$`S_{i}\in[0,100]`$, the number of turns $`T_{i}`$, and the total
encounter cost $`C_{i}`$
(Sections [3.6](#S3.SS6 "3.6 Benchmark Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark: Med-Inquire ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning")
and [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Cost Model ‣ 3 Benchmark: Med-Inquire ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning")).
In our experiments, we report mean results over the full evaluation set
of $`N`$ cases:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i},\quad\bar{T}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_{i},\quad\bar{C}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}C_{i}.
``` |  | (6) |

These three mean values summarize diagnostic correctness ($`\bar{S}`$)
and interaction efficiency ($`\bar{T}`$ and $`\bar{C}`$) under the same
turn limit $`T_{\max}`$ and the same cost table for all methods.

### 5.5 Results

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.4 Process Grader (action-level feedback) ‣ 4 Method: EvoClinician ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning")
reports mean diagnostic grade $`\bar{S}`$, mean turns $`\bar{T}`$, and
mean cost $`\bar{C}`$ under the same test-time learning setting
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Test-Time Learning Setting ‣ 4 Method: EvoClinician ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning")).
In this setting, a “self-evolving” method changes its behavior over the
case stream by updating its prompt or memory between episodes.

\(1\) Test-time learning improves not only final diagnoses, but also the
information-gathering policy. Across backbones, methods that update
across episodes improve $`\bar{S}`$ more than methods that only retrieve
past text. For example, on gemini-3-pro, memory methods move from 48.2
(Static Prompt) to 52.0 (Evo-Memory), while self-evolving methods reach
57.9 (EvoTest) and 59.8 (EvoClinician). The same ordering holds for
gpt-5.1, gpt-4o-mini, and MedGemma-27b (for example, 43.6
$`\rightarrow`$ 47.1 $`\rightarrow`$ 52.5 $`\rightarrow`$ 54.2 on
gpt-5.1, and 41.0 $`\rightarrow`$ 44.8 $`\rightarrow`$ 49.6
$`\rightarrow`$ 51.1 on MedGemma-27b). This is consistent with the idea
that the useful signal from prior episodes includes action rules (which
question to ask next, which test to avoid, and when to stop).

\(2\) Cost differences are driven by which actions are chosen, not only
by how many turns are used. Across backbones, $`\bar{T}`$ stays in a
narrow band (about 9 to 11 turns), while $`\bar{C}`$ varies more. For
example, on gemini-3-pro, EvoTest and EvoClinician use a similar number
of turns (9.4 versus 9.1) but have very different costs (1605 versus
1275). The same effect appears on gpt-5.1 (1650 versus 1310) and
MedGemma-27b (1670 versus 1328). This suggests that cost is mainly
affected by test selection (for example, ordering expensive tests early)
rather than conversation length. In a multi-turn diagnosis task,
efficiency therefore depends on learning which information to request
and when.

\(3\) The gain from self-evolving updates is smaller on weaker
backbones, which suggests that adaptation needs basic reasoning and
instruction-following ability. Absolute $`\bar{S}`$ decreases from
stronger to weaker backbones, and the improvement from adaptation also
decreases. The improvement from Static Prompt to EvoClinician is
$`+11.6`$ on gemini-3-pro (48.2 $`\rightarrow`$ 59.8), $`+10.6`$ on
gpt-5.1 (43.6 $`\rightarrow`$ 54.2), $`+10.1`$ on MedGemma-27b (41.0
$`\rightarrow`$ 51.1), and $`+9.1`$ on gpt-4o-mini (38.9 $`\rightarrow`$
48.0). This pattern is consistent with test-time learning helping most
when the backbone can already form a reasonable differential diagnosis
and can follow the multi-step update signal. On MedGemma-27b,
performance falls between gpt-5.1 and gpt-4o-mini across methods (for
example, EvoClinician $`\bar{S}=51.1`$ lies between 54.2 and 48.0),
which matches the intended positioning of this backbone in the table.

| Method (gemini-3-pro) | $`\bar{T}\downarrow`$ | Diagnose time (s)$`\downarrow`$ | Update time (s)$`\downarrow`$ | Total time (s)$`\downarrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Static Prompt | 9.8 | 11.7 | 0.0 | 11.7 |
| RAG | 10.3 | 12.4 | 0.8 | 13.2 |
| EvoTest | 9.4 | 11.3 | 7.6 | 18.9 |
| EvoClinician | 9.1 | 11.0 | 6.1 | 17.1 |

Table 2: Time efficiency on Med-Inquire (gemini-3-pro). We report mean
turns $`\bar{T}`$, mean Diagnose time (interactive episode only), mean
Update time (post-episode adaptation), and mean Total time per case. All
values are wall-clock seconds averaged over the full case stream under
the same execution and decoding settings.

| Variant (gemini-3-pro backbone) | $`\bar{S}\uparrow`$ | $`\bar{T}\downarrow`$ | $`\bar{C}\downarrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|
| EvoClinician | 59.8 | 9.1 | 1275 |
| No action-level grading | 54.6 | 9.4 | 1405 |
| Prompt evolution only | 56.7 | 9.3 | 1315 |
| Memory evolution only | 55.3 | 9.6 | 1390 |
| Yield-only grading | 58.6 | 9.2 | 1510 |
| Positive-only memory | 58.9 | 9.2 | 1300 |
| No negative memory | 57.8 | 9.2 | 1335 |

Table 3: Ablation study for EvoClinician on Med-Inquire (gemini-3-pro).
Each variant removes one element of the Diagnose–Grade–Evolve loop while
keeping the backbone model, decoding settings, case order, $`T_{\max}`$,
and the Med-Inquire environment fixed.

### 5.6 Model Analysis

Learning curves over the case stream.
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.5 Evolver (prompt and memory updates) ‣ 4 Method: EvoClinician ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning")
plots the running mean Judge grade $`\bar{S}_{1:t}`$ and running mean
cost $`\bar{C}_{1:t}`$ over the fixed stream of 915 cases. The first
$`\sim`$50–100 cases show large variance (wide bands and frequent
crossings), which is expected because the running mean is based on few
episodes and because per-case difficulty varies. After this early
region, the curves separate more clearly. EvoClinician shows a steady
increase in $`\bar{S}_{1:t}`$ and ends with the highest grade, while
also showing the strongest decrease in $`\bar{C}_{1:t}`$, reaching the
lowest cost by a clear margin. EvoTest improves grade early and remains
competitive on $`\bar{S}_{1:t}`$, but it stays consistently higher cost
than EvoClinician throughout the stream, which matches the idea that
better diagnostic grade does not automatically imply lower resource use.
Methods that only optimize prompts or use memory retrieval tend to
plateau earlier in $`\bar{S}_{1:t}`$ and show smaller cost reductions,
suggesting that cross-episode updates change action choices in a way
that affects both correctness and test ordering over time.

Ablation on key components.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.5 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning")
highlights three factors behind the gains. First, action-level grading
drives stable learning across cases: removing it (using transcript-level
feedback only) lowers both diagnostic grade and cost efficiency. This
points to better credit assignment as the main benefit, because the
system can link outcomes to specific earlier actions instead of relying
on a single end-of-episode score. Second, prompt and memory updates
serve different functions and work best together. Prompt-only evolution
lowers waste by adding general rules (cost remains close to the full
method), but it does not cover rare contexts, so accuracy drops.
Memory-only evolution reuses past actions, but without updated rules it
can retrieve mixed-quality suggestions and tends to order more tests,
which lowers both accuracy and cost efficiency. Third, cost-aware
grading is needed to avoid “accuracy by over-testing.” Yield-only
grading keeps accuracy close to the full system but increases cost,
showing that yield alone does not prevent expensive early confirmation.
Keeping negative memories also matters: removing CRITICAL_ERROR entries
hurts accuracy more than removing other negative entries, consistent
with negative items acting as constraints that help avoid repeated
unsafe or low-value patterns.

Efficiency analysis. We measure time efficiency as mean wall-clock
seconds per case under a fixed setup (single-threaded execution and
identical decoding settings). We split time into (i) Diagnose time,
spent inside the interactive episode, and (ii) Update time, spent after
the episode on grading and evolution. This split matters because
non-adaptive baselines have zero update time, while self-evolving
methods pay extra update time to improve later behavior.
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.5 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ EvoClinician: A Self-Evolving Agent for Multi-Turn Medical Diagnosis via Test-Time Evolutionary Learning")
shows that using fewer turns gives a small, consistent reduction in
Diagnose time, but total time for self-evolving methods is mainly set by
post-episode updates. EvoClinician is faster than EvoTest because
structured action-level critiques make prompt and memory edits more
targeted, which reduces update work per case. Overall, EvoClinician
increases total time per case relative to static baselines, but keeps
the update overhead lower than other self-evolving methods while
improving policies over the case stream.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced Med-Inquire, an interactive benchmark for multi-turn
medical diagnosis that forces an agent to actively gather information
through sequential questions and test orders, while tracking both
diagnostic correctness and resource cost. Unlike one-shot vignette
evaluation, Med-Inquire measures whether an agent can choose
informative, low-cost actions and decide when evidence is sufficient to
stop. We also proposed EvoClinician, a test-time self-evolving agent
based on a repeated Diagnose–Grade–Evolve loop. EvoClinician uses
action-level feedback for credit assignment and applies gradient-free
updates to both prompt rules and external memory between cases. Across
model backbones, EvoClinician improves mean diagnostic grade while
reducing turns and cost relative to memory agents and other
self-evolving baselines. Ablations indicate that action-level grading
and cost-aware feedback are both necessary to avoid accuracy gains
driven by over-testing, and that prompt and memory updates contribute in
complementary ways.

## Impact Statement

This paper presents Med-Inquire, a benchmark for multi-turn medical
diagnosis, and EvoClinician, a test-time learning agent that updates
prompt rules and external memory between cases using action-level
feedback on clinical yield (how much an action reduces uncertainty) and
resource efficiency (cost and steps). The main expected benefit is for
research on interactive diagnostic strategies that can improve
diagnostic accuracy while limiting unnecessary tests, supported by
reproducible logs and per-action feedback. Key limits and risks remain:
Med-Inquire is a simulation in which the Patient agent may generate
plausible but unverified details when case reports omit information, so
benchmark scores do not establish clinical safety or readiness for use
with patients. Test-time updates can also shift behavior over time in
hard-to-predict ways if grading is noisy or biased, and medical language
model outputs can be misused for self-diagnosis or treated with undue
confidence. Bias may come from the published-case data source and from
model-based grading, and the cost table is only a proxy that does not
match real billing, so cost results should not be used as billing
advice; any real-world use would require clinical validation,
monitoring, and strong safeguards.

## Appendix C Reproduction details for Med-Inquire and EvoClinician

This appendix reports the environment interfaces, grading rules,
prompts, data records, and update steps used by Med-Inquire and
EvoClinician. The goal is that an independent group can rebuild the
benchmark and run the same Diagnose–Grade–Evolve loop under the same
assumptions.

### C.1 What must be logged for a reproducible run

A run should log the exact identifiers of all language models used for
the Actor, Patient, Examination, Judge, Process Grader, and Evolver. It
should also log decoding settings (temperature, top-$`p`$, max tokens),
the maximum number of turns $`T_{\max}`$, the case order over the $`N`$
episodes, the cost table version, the action parsing rules, the memory
budget $`B_{M}`$, the prompt rule budget $`B_{P}`$, the retrieval count
$`k`$, and the embedding model and index settings used for retrieval. If
any component uses randomness (for example, Patient free-text generation
when a fact is missing), the run should log the seed and should cache
within-episode generated details.

## Appendix D Med-Inquire environment

### D.1 Hidden case file and initial abstract

Each episode corresponds to one clinical case. The environment stores a
hidden case file with at least these fields: (i) case information, (ii)
physical examination, (iii) diagnostic tests, and (iv) final diagnosis.
The agent sees only an initial abstract at the start of the episode (for
example, chief complaint and basic demographics if present). All other
details are returned only through actions.

### D.2 Actions and observations

At each turn $`t`$, the agent selects one action $`a_{t}`$ from
AskQuestion, OrderTest, and SubmitDiagnosis. The environment returns an
observation $`o_{t+1}`$ and updates the running cost by $`c(a_{t})`$.
The episode ends when SubmitDiagnosis is taken or when $`t=T_{\max}`$,
in which case the environment forces submission using the latest draft
diagnosis from the agent.

To make parsing deterministic, the environment should require a fixed
machine-readable action format. One simple option is JSON with two
fields: action_type and action_text. The environment should define one
fixed behavior when parsing fails (for example, one reformat request
that does not count as a turn, or a no-op that counts as a turn). This
choice should be held constant across all methods in a comparison.

### D.3 Transcript record format

Each episode transcript is logged as an ordered list of turn records.
Each record should contain the turn index, the action type, the action
text, the environment response, and the cost applied at that turn. A
minimal JSON record format is:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### D.4 Patient agent

The Patient agent answers symptom and history questions using only
information in the hidden case file. When the case file does not include
the requested detail, the Patient agent generates a medically reasonable
patient-style answer that stays consistent with (i) the case diagnosis
and (ii) information already revealed in the same episode. These
generated details should be cached and reused later in the episode to
prevent contradictions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### D.5 Examination agent

The Examination agent returns results for physical examination items and
diagnostic tests. If the requested test is recorded in the case file,
the agent returns the recorded result. If it is not recorded, it returns
NOT AVAILABLE and does not invent results.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### D.6 Cost estimator

Med-Inquire assigns a non-negative cost to each action. The total cost
is

|     |                           |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       C=\sum_{t=1}^{T}c(a_{t}).
       ```                        |     | (7) |

Costs should include (i) a base per-turn interaction cost and (ii) a
test-specific cost for OrderTest. Costs are reported in normalized units
so that the same schedule can be used across all cases in a run.

A cost table should be stored in a versioned file and should support
alias matching so that small wording changes do not avoid cost. A
minimal CSV-like schema is:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before lookup, the environment should normalize test names by
lowercasing, trimming whitespace, and mapping common variants using the
alias column. If a request does not match any entry, the environment
should apply one fixed default cost for unknown tests and still return
NOT AVAILABLE from the Examination agent.

## Appendix E Diagnosis judging

### E.1 Rubric

The Judge assigns a graded correctness score $`S\in[0,100]`$ based on
clinical match to the hidden ground-truth diagnosis. The rubric used in
the main paper is reproduced here:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.2 Judge agent prompt

For reproducibility, the Judge should run with deterministic decoding.
The Judge compares the submission to the ground truth after simple
normalization (lowercasing, whitespace cleanup, and a fixed abbreviation
map). The prompt below produces a score and a brief justification.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix F EvoClinician agent loop

### F.1 Actor prompt

The Actor is an LLM agent that (i) interacts with the environment, (ii)
tracks a running differential diagnosis, and (iii) decides when to stop
and submit. The Actor prompt is a base instruction plus a rule list that
can be edited between episodes. The prompt also contains the required
action format.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### F.2 Process Grader prompt (action-level feedback)

The Process Grader performs post-episode credit assignment. It labels
each action using both clinical yield and resource efficiency. The
output is used only as an update signal, not as ground truth.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### F.3 Evolver prompt (prompt rules and memory updates)

The Evolver updates (i) the Actor rule list and (ii) an external memory
store. Rule edits aim to change general action selection. Memory entries
store situation-action-outcome items with a quality label. Budgets
$`B_{P}`$ and $`B_{M}`$ limit growth.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### F.4 Memory storage format

Each memory item stores a compressed context, the action, the outcome,
and the grade. A minimal JSON schema is:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The environment should update retrieval counters so that deletion can
depend on reuse.

### F.5 Retrieval method

At turn $`t`$, the Actor retrieves $`k`$ memory items that are most
similar to the current context. Similarity can be implemented using text
embeddings and cosine similarity. The system should log the embedding
model name, embedding dimension, index type (for example, brute force or
approximate nearest neighbor), and any index parameters.

To reduce leakage from future turns, the query text for retrieval should
be derived only from the dialogue history up to turn $`t`$. One
practical choice is to build the query from a short state summary plus
the latest observation.

### F.6 Budgeted memory deletion

When memory reaches budget $`B_{M}`$, the system deletes items with low
expected reuse. One simple scoring function combines age and reuse
count:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{keep\_score}(m)=\alpha\cdot\log(1+\text{times\_retrieved}(m))-\beta\cdot\text{age}(m),
``` |  | (8) |

where age is measured in episodes since creation. The system deletes
items with the lowest keep_score until size is under budget. The
constants $`\alpha`$ and $`\beta`$ should be fixed before evaluation.

## Appendix H Metrics

For episode $`i`$, the benchmark records Judge grade
$`S_{i}\in[0,100]`$, turns $`T_{i}`$, and total cost $`C_{i}`$. Over
$`N`$ cases, reported means are:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i},\quad\bar{T}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_{i},\quad\bar{C}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}C_{i}.
``` |  | (9) |

For learning curves, the running mean up to case $`t`$ is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{S}_{1:t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}S_{i},\quad\bar{C}_{1:t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}C_{i}.
``` |  | (10) |

If uncertainty bands are plotted, the code should state whether it uses
standard error over the first $`t`$ samples and how it handles
non-independence due to adaptation.

## Appendix I Wall-clock time measurement

Time per case should be measured with the same execution settings across
methods. We separate (i) Diagnose time, which includes all interactive
turns up to submission, and (ii) Update time, which includes
post-episode grading and evolution. The measurement code should exclude
dataset loading and model warm-up, or it should include them for all
methods in the same way. The run should report hardware type and whether
calls were batched or parallel.

## Appendix J Notes on safety and interpretation

Med-Inquire is a controlled simulation. The Patient agent may generate
missing details that are consistent with the case but were not
documented in the original report. These generated details support
interaction but are not ground-truth facts. For this reason, benchmark
scores measure performance in this simulation and do not validate
clinical safety.

EvoClinician updates prompts and memory using model-generated critiques.
This can drift if the Process Grader is inconsistent. The system
therefore needs fixed budgets, fixed deletion rules, and deterministic
decoding for grading components where possible. These controls improve
auditability, but they do not make the system suitable for patient care.

## Appendix K Theory: Process Grader for Action-Level Feedback

Med-Inquire gives a sparse outcome signal: after SubmitDiagnosis, the
Judge returns a graded correctness score $`S\in[0,100]`$, and the Cost
Estimator returns a total resource cost $`C\geq 0`$. The Process Grader
adds a dense learning signal by assigning an action-level label to each
turn in the interaction transcript. This section describes a formal view
of the grader, what it is trying to estimate, and how cost enters the
feedback.

### K.1 Interaction model and objective

We model one episode as a partially observable decision process. Let
$`h_{t}`$ be the dialogue history (all prior actions and observations)
available to the Actor before turn $`t`$. The Actor chooses an action
$`a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}`$, where
$`\mathcal{A}=\{\texttt{AskQuestion},\texttt{OrderTest},\texttt{SubmitDiagnosis}\}`$,
and the environment returns an observation $`o_{t+1}`$. Each action has
a non-negative cost $`c(a_{t})\geq 0`$. The transcript is

|     |                                                    |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \tau=\{(h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1},c(a_{t}))\}_{t=1}^{T},
       ```                                                 |     | (11) |

where $`T`$ is the number of turns until submission.

The benchmark returns a final diagnostic grade $`S(\tau)`$ and total
cost

|     |                                 |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       C(\tau)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}c(a_{t}).
       ```                              |     | (12) |

A cost-aware scalar objective for one episode can be written as

|     |                                  |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       J(\tau)=S(\tau)-\lambda C(\tau),
       ```                               |     | (13) |

where $`\lambda\geq 0`$ controls the score–cost tradeoff. The Actor does
not observe $`S(\tau)`$ until the end, so learning which earlier actions
helped is a credit assignment problem.

### K.2 What the grader estimates: marginal value of an action

In an ideal setting with a known environment model, one could define a
state-value function and action-value function for histories:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V(h_{t})=\mathbb{E}[J(\tau)\mid h_{t}],\quad Q(h_{t},a_{t})=\mathbb{E}[J(\tau)\mid h_{t},a_{t}].
``` |  | (14) |

The marginal contribution of action $`a_{t}`$ at history $`h_{t}`$ is
the advantage

|     |                                         |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       A(h_{t},a_{t})=Q(h_{t},a_{t})-V(h_{t}).
       ```                                      |     | (15) |

If $`A(h_{t},a_{t})>0`$, the action is better than an average
alternative at that point; if $`A(h_{t},a_{t})<0`$, it is worse. In
Med-Inquire we do not have $`Q`$ and $`V`$ in closed form, so the
Process Grader acts as an estimator that maps $`(\tau,S,C)`$ to per-turn
feedback. We denote this estimate by $`\widehat{A}_{t}`$, computed from
the text transcript plus the final Judge score and the cost report:

|     |                                         |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{A}_{t}=G_{\theta}(\tau,S,C;t),
       ```                                      |     | (16) |

where $`G_{\theta}`$ is the grader model with parameters $`\theta`$ (in
practice, a language model prompt plus decoding settings).

### K.3 A cost-aware view through information gain

A second way to motivate action-level labels is through diagnostic
uncertainty. Let $`D`$ be the (unknown) true diagnosis. Given history
$`h_{t}`$, define a belief distribution $`b_{t}(d)=P(D=d\mid h_{t})`$
over diagnoses $`d`$. The uncertainty in $`b_{t}`$ can be measured by
Shannon entropy:

|     |                                          |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       H(b_{t})=-\sum_{d}b_{t}(d)\log b_{t}(d).
       ```                                       |     | (17) |

After action $`a_{t}`$ produces observation $`o_{t+1}`$, the belief
updates to $`b_{t+1}`$, and the information gain from the action is

|     |                                      |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{IG}_{t}=H(b_{t})-H(b_{t+1}).
       ```                                   |     | (18) |

An efficiency score that accounts for resource use is the information
gain per unit cost:

|     |                                                     |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \eta_{t}=\frac{\mathrm{IG}_{t}}{c(a_{t})+\epsilon},
       ```                                                  |     | (19) |

where $`\epsilon>0`$ avoids division by zero. In Med-Inquire, the grader
does not compute $`b_{t}`$ exactly. Instead, it approximates whether the
new observation reduced uncertainty in a clinically meaningful way, and
it compares that reduction to the action cost and to cheaper
alternatives that could have produced similar reduction.

### K.4 Label assignment as a thresholded decision rule

The Process Grader outputs a discrete label $`g_{t}\in\mathcal{G}`$ for
each turn, where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{G}=\{\texttt{HIGH\_YIELD},\texttt{LOW\_YIELD},\texttt{INEFFICIENT},\texttt{CRITICAL\_ERROR}\}.
``` |  | (20) |

One simple theoretical rule is to base labels on two latent quantities:
(1) estimated clinical value $`\widehat{v}_{t}`$ (how much the action
reduced diagnostic uncertainty or improved correctness), and (2)
estimated efficiency $`\widehat{\eta}_{t}`$ (value relative to cost).
With thresholds $`\alpha_{1}>\alpha_{0}\geq 0`$ and $`\beta>0`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{t}=\begin{cases}\texttt{CRITICAL\_ERROR}&\text{if the action increases risk or blocks correct diagnosis (safety failure)}\\
\texttt{HIGH\_YIELD}&\text{if }\widehat{v}_{t}\geq\alpha_{1}\text{ and }\widehat{\eta}_{t}\geq\beta\\
\texttt{INEFFICIENT}&\text{if }\widehat{v}_{t}\geq\alpha_{0}\text{ and }\widehat{\eta}_{t}<\beta\\
\texttt{LOW\_YIELD}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
``` |  | (21) |

This matches the intended meaning in the benchmark: an action can be
helpful but still inefficient if a lower-cost question or test would
likely give similar information. A CRITICAL_ERROR label is reserved for
actions that are unsafe or that strongly push the trajectory away from a
correct diagnosis given the information available at that time (to
reduce hindsight bias).

### K.5 Assumptions and limits

This theory relies on three assumptions. First, transcript text contains
enough detail for a grader to judge whether information reduced
uncertainty. Second, the Judge score $`S`$ is a reasonable proxy for
correctness, even though it is computed from text matching under a
rubric rather than from patient outcomes. Third, cost values reflect
relative resource use in a stable way across cases.

In practice, $`\widehat{A}_{t}`$, $`\widehat{v}_{t}`$, and
$`\widehat{\eta}_{t}`$ are noisy because they are inferred from text and
because the case file may not include all details that a clinician would
normally use. For this reason, the grader output should be treated as a
learning signal for the Evolver rather than as ground truth. The use of
discrete labels also trades accuracy for stability: coarse labels reduce
sensitivity to small grader errors but cannot represent fine differences
between similar actions.
````
